title: Explain an API with success and failure paths
goal: Map a request and response without exposing credentials or inventing a service’s internals.
explanation: An API is an agreed interface, not a window into every internal system. Use an invented service so you can distinguish the known contract from implementation guesses. Include authentication, permissions, status codes, rate limits and data minimization. A diagram is not a connected API call.
sampleInput: Fictional contract: GET /playlists/p01 with a valid authorized token returns {"id":"p01","tracks":["t01","t02"]}. Missing/invalid token → 401. Valid token without access → 403. Missing playlist → 404. Too many requests → 429 with a retry hint. No real service or credential is involved.
prompt: Explain this fictional API in plain language as a request/response flow. Include the five outcomes, what the client should display and what it must not log. Distinguish authentication from permission. Do not invent a real music service’s endpoints or internal architecture.
workedExample: 401 means credentials are missing/invalid; 403 means the supplied identity lacks access. A 429 should not trigger an endless tight retry loop. Tokens belong in protected request handling, not screenshots, URLs, analytics or shared exercise notes.

steps.title: Read the contract
steps.text: Separate endpoint, method, credentials, allowed response fields and status codes.

steps.title: Build a success flow
steps.text: Trace the fictional mobile app’s request and the returned track IDs.

steps.title: Add the four failure routes
steps.text: Write a safe message and next action for 401, 403, 404 and 429.

steps.title: Minimize the log
steps.text: Keep status, timing and a non-secret request ID; omit tokens and unnecessary personal data.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.text: Explain the difference between authentication and permission using the two relevant statuses.

checks: Success and all four failure outcomes appear in the flow.
401 and 403 are distinguished and rate limiting has a bounded retry/wait policy.
The artifact is labelled a contract simulation and contains no real tokens or invented live endpoints.
commonMistakes: Confusing a valid login with permission to read every resource.
Putting API keys in query strings or shared screenshots.
offline: Move request/status cards through the flow and explain the client’s next action for each.
reflection: Which error should lead to a permission review rather than another login attempt?

evidence.title: Keep the build
evidence.detail: Save your original input, exact prompt and resulting artifact. Success and all four failure outcomes appear in the flow.

evidence.title: Show what you tested
evidence.detail: Record a pass/fail result and evidence for every check below. 401 and 403 are distinguished and rate limiting has a bounded retry/wait policy.

evidence.title: Explain a limitation
evidence.detail: Write what changed after one deliberate revision and name a remaining failure mode. Confusing a valid login with permission to read every resource.
